title: R for Clinical Data Science
text:
Preface
This book is a personal reference guide to R for clinical data science, written and maintained by Thibault Dupont. It consolidates notes from various courses, workshops, and hands-on projects — covering R fundamentals, data wrangling, visualization, statistics, and machine learning — with a focus on applications relevant to clinical research and intensive care medicine.
The book is structured to be read linearly for a first pass, or used as a reference when you need to look up a specific technique. Each chapter includes explanatory text, annotated code, and practical examples.
How to use this book

New to R? Start at Chapter 1 and read through Chapter 5.
Refreshing data wrangling? Jump to Chapter 4 (dplyr) and Chapter 6 (ggplot2).
Working on a clinical study? Chapters 7–10 cover the stats you will use most: descriptive tables, regression, survival analysis, and contingency tables.
Building a dashboard or app? Chapter 14 covers Shiny.

Technical setup
All code in this book runs with R ≥ 4.2. Package dependencies are loaded at the top of each chapter. The tidyverse meta-package covers most of what is needed.

install.packages("tidyverse")

title: 1  R Basics
text:
1.1.1 Useful utility functions
A handful of functions you will reach for constantly when exploring any R session or dataset.

# R version info
version
major <- version$major
minor <- version$minor

# Package version
packageVersion('caret')

# Print column names in a reusable format
dput(colnames(data))



1.1.2 Hardware benchmarking
The benchmarkme package lets you check your machine’s performance relative to other R users — useful when deciding whether to run heavy computations locally or on a cluster.

library(benchmarkme)

# Standard benchmark (arithmetic, matrix operations, etc.)
res <- benchmark_std(runs = 3)
plot(res)

# RAM and CPU info
get_ram()
get_cpu()

# I/O benchmark (time to read a 50MB file)
res_io <- benchmark_io(runs = 1, size = 50)
plot(res_io)



1.1.3 Core data formats
R has two main binary formats for storing objects:

.csv — plain text, portable, human-readable
.rds — R’s native binary format; preserves object class exactly


read.csv("data.csv")     # returns a data.frame
readRDS("data.rds")      # returns whatever was saved

title: 1  R Basics
text:
1.2 Vectors
Vectors are the fundamental unit in R. Everything is built on them.

# Inspect any object
str(gapminder)
class(gapminder)
glimpse(gapminder)    # tidyverse equivalent

# Dimensions
dim(mpg)
head(mpg)
tail(mpg)

# Access a function from a specific package
dplyr::glimpse(gapminder)

# Combine elements
x <- c(1, 2, 3)

# Vector arithmetic is element-wise
c(1, 2, 3) * c(7, 6, 5)

# Sequences
seq(1, 5, by = 1)
1:5


1.2.1 Functions applied to vectors

sort(x)       # sort ascending
rev(x)        # reverse order
unique(x)     # remove duplicates
table(x)      # frequency table

# Replicate
rep("ABC", times = 3)



1.2.2 Indexing
R uses 1-based indexing. Be careful: x[1] returns the first element, not the second.

# Named vector
x <- c(e = 2.718, pi = 3.14, sqrt2 = 1.414)
x[c("e", "pi")]
x[c(1, 3)]

# Matrix indexing
mat <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2)
mat[1, ]     # first row
mat[, 2]     # second column

# List access
my_list <- list(a = 1:3, b = "hello")
my_list$a
my_list[["a"]]



1.2.3 Sorting and ordering

library(dslabs)
data("murders")

sort(murders$total)          # returns sorted values
order(murders$total)         # returns indices of sorted values
rank(murders$total)          # returns rank of each element

# Sort a data frame by a column
murders[order(murders$total), ]



1.2.4 Type coercion
R will coerce types silently, which can cause subtle bugs. Always check your types.

b <- c(1, "b", 3)
class(b)        # "character" — 1 and 3 were coerced

# Explicit coercion
as.numeric(b)    # NAs introduced for non-numeric values
as.character(42)
as.factor(c("low", "medium", "high"))
as.data.frame(mat)



1.2.5 Factors and ordered variables
Factors represent categorical variables. Ordered factors carry additional information about the direction of the levels.

# Unordered factor (nominal)
survey <- c("M", "F", "F", "M", "M")
factor_survey <- factor(survey)
levels(factor_survey)

# Renaming levels — order must match the current order of levels
levels(factor_survey) <- c("Female", "Male")

# Ordered factor (ordinal)
temp <- c("Low", "Medium", "High", "Low", "High")
temp_fct <- factor(temp, levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High"), ordered = TRUE)
temp_fct

title: 2  R Markdown & Quarto
text:
2.1 Document structure
R Markdown (.Rmd) and its successor Quarto (.qmd) let you weave together prose, code, and output into a single reproducible document. This chapter covers everything you need to author and customise these documents effectively.
Every R Markdown / Quarto document has three parts:

title: 2  R Markdown & Quarto
text:
YAML header — metadata at the top, delimited by ---
Text — prose written in Markdown
Code chunks — executable blocks surrounded by backticks


2.1.1 The YAML header
---
title: "My Analysis"
author: "Thibault Dupont"
date: "2026-05-09"
output:
  html_document:
    toc: true
    toc_depth: 2
    toc_float:
      collapsed: false
      smooth_scroll: true
    number_sections: true
---
Key YAML options:



Option
Effect




toc: true
Adds a table of contents


toc_depth: 2
TOC shows headers up to ## only


toc_float
TOC floats on the left side while scrolling


number_sections: true
Automatically numbers sections



Automatic dates:
date: "2026-05-09"
date: "09 May 2026"
date: "Last edited on: 2026-05-09"
Multiple output formats:
output:
  html_document: default
  pdf_document: default
  word_document: default

title: 2  R Markdown & Quarto
text:
2.2 The setup chunk
The first code chunk in a document is usually the setup chunk. It sets global options that apply to every subsequent chunk.

title: 2  R Markdown & Quarto
text:
2.3 Code chunks

2.3.1 Essential chunk options



Option
Effect




echo = FALSE
Hides the code, shows the output


eval = FALSE
Shows the code but does not run it


include = FALSE
Runs the code silently; no code or output shown


collapse = TRUE
Merges code and output into a single block


message = FALSE
Suppresses package loading messages


warning = FALSE
Suppresses warnings





2.3.2 Figure options
#| fig.width: 8
#| fig.height: 5
#| fig.align: "center"
#| fig.cap: "Distribution of life expectancy by continent"
#| out.width: "70%"
These can also be set globally in the setup chunk.

title: 2  R Markdown & Quarto
text:
2.4 Text formatting

2.4.1 Basic Markdown
# Heading 1
## Heading 2
### Heading 3

**bold text**
*italic text*
`inline code`
~~strikethrough~~

- Bullet item
- Another item

1. First numbered item
2. Second numbered item


2.4.2 Links and images
[Link text](https://www.example.com)
![Alt text](path/to/image.png)


2.4.3 Inline R code
Embed a variable directly in text by opening a backtick, writing the letter r followed by a space, then any R expression, then a closing backtick. For example, writing nrow(df) as an inline expression will print the number of rows directly in your sentence: The model included 248 patients.

title: 2  R Markdown & Quarto
text:
2.5 Parameterised reports
Parameters make it easy to re-run the same report for different subgroups or time periods without editing the code.
Define parameters in YAML:
params:
  country: "France"
  year: 2023
  start_date: "2023-01-01"
Use them in code:
params$country
params$year
Use them in text by embedding inline R expressions in your prose — for example, params$country and params$year inserted inline will print the parameter values directly into the sentence when the document is rendered.

title: 3  Data Import & I/O
text:
3.1 Plain-text files
This chapter covers reading and writing data in R, from plain-text files to Excel workbooks and SQL databases.

title: 3  Data Import & I/O
text:
3.1.1 The readr package (recommended)
readr functions are faster and more consistent than base R equivalents. They return tibbles and provide helpful parsing messages.



Function
Equivalent to
Separator




read_csv()
read.csv()
Comma


read_tsv()
read.delim()
Tab


read_csv2()
read.csv2()
Semicolon (European)


read_delim()
read.table()
Any delimiter


read_fwf()
—
Fixed-width


read_rds()
readRDS()
R binary




# Basic import
df <- read_csv("data.csv")

# Control parsing explicitly
df <- read_csv(
  "data.csv",
  col_types = list(
    age   = col_integer(),
    score = col_double(),
    group = col_factor()
  ),
  skip   = 1,    # skip the first row
  n_max  = 500   # read only 500 rows
)

# Read only specific columns
df <- read_csv("data.csv", col_types = cols_only(id = col_character(), age = col_integer()))



3.1.2 Reading multiple files at once

# Stack multiple CSV files with a filename identifier column
files <- c("data/01-cohort.csv", "data/02-cohort.csv", "data/03-cohort.csv")
combined <- read_csv(files, id = "source_file")



3.1.3 Manual data entry

# tibble() works column by column
tibble(
  id    = 1:3,
  group = c("A", "B", "A"),
  score = c(82.1, 74.5, 90.2)
)

# tribble() works row by row — easier to read for small tables
tribble(
  ~id, ~group, ~score,
    1,   "A",   82.1,
    2,   "B",   74.5,
    3,   "A",   90.2
)



3.1.4 Column type cheatsheet



Collector
Type




col_double()
Numeric (floating point)


col_integer()
Integer


col_character()
String


col_factor()
Categorical


col_logical()
TRUE / FALSE


col_date()
Date (ISO 8601)


col_datetime()
Date + time


col_skip()
Skip this column





3.1.5 Parsing helpers

# Extract a number from a messy string
parse_number("$1,234.56")   # → 1234.56
parse_number("12 patients") # → 12

# Fix a column containing "five" as text
df <- df |>
  mutate(age = parse_number(if_else(age == "five", "5", age)))

3.2 Writing files

write_csv(df, "output/results.csv")
write_tsv(df, "output/results.tsv")
write_rds(df, "output/results.rds")        # preserves R object exactly

title: 3  Data Import & I/O
text:
3.3 Excel files

3.3.1 Reading with readxl

library(readxl)

# List available sheets
excel_sheets("workbook.xlsx")

# Read a specific sheet
df <- read_excel("workbook.xlsx", sheet = "Sheet1")

# Read all sheets at once
all_sheets <- lapply(
  excel_sheets("workbook.xlsx"),
  read_excel,
  path = "workbook.xlsx"
)

# Specify column names when the file has no header row
df <- read_excel(
  "data.xlsx",
  sheet     = 1,
  col_names = c("country", paste0("year_", 1960:1966))
)



3.3.2 Writing with openxlsx

library(openxlsx)
write.xlsx(df, "output.xlsx", sheetName = "Results")

title: 3  Data Import & I/O
text:
3.4 SQL databases
R can connect to any SQL database via DBI with a database-specific driver.

library(DBI)
library(RMySQL)

# Open a connection
con <- dbConnect(
  MySQL(),
  dbname   = "clinical_db",
  host     = "server.hospital.fr",
  port     = 3306,
  user     = "analyst",
  password = Sys.getenv("DB_PASSWORD")  # never hard-code passwords
)

# List tables
dbListTables(con)

# Import a full table
patients <- dbReadTable(con, "patients")

# Import all tables at once
tables <- lapply(dbListTables(con), dbReadTable, conn = con)

# SQL query
results <- dbGetQuery(con, "
  SELECT name, admission_date
  FROM patients
  WHERE icu_los > 2
    AND year(admission_date) = 2022
")

# Chunked import (useful for large tables)
res <- dbSendQuery(con, "SELECT * FROM lab_results WHERE patient_id > 1000")
chunk <- dbFetch(res, n = 500)   # fetch 500 rows at a time
dbClearResult(res)

# Always disconnect when done
dbDisconnect(con)

text:
3.5 Input / output utilities

3.5.1 Console and file output

# print() adds a [1] prefix
print(c(1, 2, 3))

# cat() is cleaner for formatted output; writes to file with the file= argument
cat("Hello, world\n")
cat(c(1, 2, 3), file = "output.txt", sep = "\n")
cat(c(4, 5, 6), file = "output.txt", sep = "\n", append = TRUE)

# sink() redirects all console output to a file
sink("log.txt")
summary(df)
sink()  # restore console output



3.5.2 File system

list.files()                        # files in working directory
list.files(all.files = TRUE)        # include hidden files
list.files("data/", pattern = "*.csv", full.names = TRUE)



3.5.3 Reading tabular text with base R

# read.table() is the general base R function; all other base readers wrap it
df <- read.table("data.txt", header = TRUE, sep = "\t", dec = ".")

# Shortcuts
read.csv("data.csv")              # sep = ",", dec = "."
read.csv2("data.csv")             # sep = ";", dec = ","
read.delim("data.txt")            # sep = "\t", dec = "."

library(pdftools)

url <- "https://example.com/paper.pdf"
temp <- tempfile(fileext = ".pdf")

title: 4  Data Wrangling with dplyr
text:
4.1 The pipe
dplyr is the core tool for data manipulation in R. Its verbs are organised around what they operate on: rows, columns, groups, or tables.
# Base R pipe (R ≥ 4.1)
data |> filter(year == 2007) |> summarise(mean_life = mean(lifeExp))

# Tidyverse pipe (magrittr) — equivalent
data %>% filter(year == 2007) %>% summarise(mean_life = mean(lifeExp))

title: 4  Data Wrangling with dplyr
text:
4.2 Row verbs

4.2.1 filter() — keep rows matching a condition

# Single condition
gapminder |> filter(continent == "Africa")

# Multiple conditions (AND)
gapminder |> filter(continent == "Africa", year == 2012, lifeExp >= 70)

# OR
gapminder |> filter(continent == "Africa" | continent == "Asia")

# %in% for multiple values
years    <- c(1990, 2000, 2007)
countries <- c("Vietnam", "France")
gapminder |> filter(year %in% years, country %in% countries)



4.2.2 arrange() — reorder rows

gapminder |> arrange(lifeExp)           # ascending
gapminder |> arrange(desc(lifeExp))     # descending
gapminder |> arrange(continent, desc(gdpPercap))  # multi-column



4.2.3 distinct() — remove duplicate rows

# Unique rows overall
df |> distinct()

# Unique combinations of specific columns
df |> distinct(country, continent, .keep_all = TRUE)



4.2.4 slice_*() — extract rows by position

df |> slice_max(lifeExp, n = 5)     # top 5 rows by life expectancy
df |> slice_min(gdpPercap, n = 3)   # bottom 3 rows by GDP
df |> slice_head(n = 10)             # first 10 rows
df |> slice_sample(n = 100)          # random 100 rows

title: 4  Data Wrangling with dplyr
text:
4.3 Column verbs

4.3.1 select() — choose columns

# By name
df |> select(country, year, lifeExp)

# By position
df |> select(1:3)

# Helper functions
df |> select(starts_with("gdp"))
df |> select(ends_with("_mm"))
df |> select(contains("life"))
df |> select(matches("\\.t\\."))      # regex

# Everything except
df |> select(-country, -year)
df |> select(-(col1:col4))

# Type-based selection
df |> select(where(is.numeric))
df |> select(where(is.character))



4.3.2 mutate() — add or transform columns

# New column at the end
gapminder |> mutate(gdp_total = gdpPercap * pop)

# Control placement
gapminder |> mutate(gdp_total = gdpPercap * pop, .after = year)
gapminder |> mutate(gdp_total = gdpPercap * pop, .before = 1)

# Keep only used columns
flights |>
  mutate(
    gain          = dep_delay - arr_delay,
    gain_per_hour = gain / (air_time / 60),
    .keep = "used"
  )

# case_when for conditional recoding
df |> mutate(
  age_group = case_when(
    age < 18  ~ "Paediatric",
    age < 65  ~ "Adult",
    .default  = "Elderly"
  )
)

# Rename a column via rename() inside a pipeline with a new name
games |> mutate(
  cat_label = case_when(
    category == "avg_us_viewers"     ~ "Average US viewers",
    category == "rating_household"   ~ "Household rating",
    category == "ad_cost"            ~ "Ad cost (USD)",
    .default                         = as.character(category)
  )
)



4.3.3 rename() — rename columns

df |> rename(new_name = old_name)
df |> janitor::clean_names()   # snake_case all column names automatically



4.3.4 relocate() — move columns

df |> relocate(score, .before = age)
df |> relocate(id, .after = last_col())

title: 4  Data Wrangling with dplyr
text:
4.4 Grouped operations

4.4.1 group_by() + summarise()

gapminder |>
  filter(year == 2007) |>
  group_by(continent) |>
  summarise(
    total_pop    = sum(pop),
    median_life  = median(lifeExp),
    mean_gdp     = mean(gdpPercap),
    n_countries  = n()
  )


  




# Multiple grouping variables
gapminder |>
  group_by(continent, year) |>
  summarise(
    median_gdp     = median(gdpPercap),
    median_lifeExp = median(lifeExp),
    .groups = "drop"
  )



4.4.2 Useful summary functions



Function
Description




n()
Count rows in group


n_distinct(x)
Count unique values of x


mean(x, na.rm=TRUE)
Mean


median(x, na.rm=TRUE)
Median


sd(x, na.rm=TRUE)
Standard deviation


first(x), last(x), nth(x, 3)
Positional values





4.4.3 count() — quick frequency tables

df |> count(group)                    # equivalent to group_by() + summarise(n = n())
df |> count(group, sort = TRUE)       # sorted descending
df |> count(group, wt = population)   # weighted count



4.4.4 top_n() within groups

# Counties with highest total population in each metro category
counties |>
  group_by(state, metro) |>
  summarise(total_pop = sum(population)) |>
  top_n(1, total_pop) |>
  ungroup() |>
  count(metro)



4.4.5 Gotcha: variable name conflicts in functions
When writing functions that use dplyr verbs, avoid naming function arguments the same as column names. Use a . prefix convention:

# BAD: filter(year == year) matches nothing
get_top_names_broken <- function(year, sex) {
  babynames |> filter(year == year, sex == sex)  # bug!
}

# GOOD: prefix function arguments with .
get_top_names <- function(.year, .sex) {
  babynames |> filter(year == .year, sex == .sex)
}

title: 4  Data Wrangling with dplyr
text:
4.5 Pivoting data
Tidy data has one variable per column, one observation per row, one value per cell. pivot_longer() and pivot_wider() move data between wide and long formats.

4.5.1 pivot_longer() — wide → long

# Weekly chart positions stored in columns wk1, wk2, ..., wk76
billboard |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols       = starts_with("wk"),
    names_to   = "week",
    values_to  = "rank",
    values_drop_na = TRUE
  ) |>
  mutate(week = parse_number(week))


# Multiple variables encoded in column names
# e.g. columns like "dob_child1", "name_child1", "dob_child2", "name_child2"
household |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = !family,
    names_to  = c(".value", "child"),  # .value tells pivot to use the prefix as the new column name
    names_sep = "_",
    values_drop_na = TRUE
  )



4.5.2 pivot_wider() — long → wide

cms_patient_experience |>
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols     = starts_with("org"),
    names_from  = measure_cd,
    values_from = prf_rate
  )

4  Data Wrangling with dplyr
text:
4.7 Data cleaning helpers

4.7.1 Missing values

# Detect
is.na(df$age)
sum(is.na(df))              # total NAs
any(is.na(df))              # any NAs?
colSums(is.na(df))          # NAs per column

# Complete cases only
df[complete.cases(df), ]
na.omit(df)

# Replace specific values with NA
df$score[df$score == 999] <- NA



4.7.2 Dates with lubridate

library(lubridate)

ymd("2024-03-15")
ymd_hms("2024-03-15 08:30:00")
dmy("15/03/2024")



4.7.3 Strings with stringr
All stringr functions start with str_ and take a string vector as first argument.

library(stringr)

str_trim("  excess whitespace  ")     # trim leading/trailing spaces
str_pad("123", width = 6, pad = "0") # "000123"
str_detect(x, "pattern")             # logical: does the pattern appear?
str_count(x, "a")                    # count occurrences
str_subset(x, "ICU")                 # keep strings matching pattern
str_replace(x, "old", "new")         # replace first match
str_replace_all(x, "old", "new")     # replace all matches
str_sub(x, 1, 4)                     # extract characters 1–4
str_length(x)                        # number of characters

# Splitting
str_split(x, fixed(" - "), n = 2, simplify = TRUE)



4.7.4 String concatenation

# paste() default separator is a space; paste0() default is ""
paste("Hello", "world", sep = " ")
paste0("patient_", 1:3)           # "patient_1" "patient_2" "patient_3"

# str_c() from stringr: propagates NA (better for data pipelines)
str_c("Hello", NA)  # NA  (paste() would give "Hello NA")
str_c(c("a", "b", "c"), collapse = ", ")  # "a, b, c"



4.7.5 Number formatting

format(3.14159, digits = 3)                # "3.14"
format(1234567, big.mark = ",")            # "1,234,567"
formatC(0.001234, format = "e", digits = 2) # "1.23e-03"
formatC(3.14159, format = "f", digits = 2)  # "3.14"

4.9 Collapsing boolean columns into a single factor
A common pattern in clinical data: you have several mutually exclusive binary columns (e.g. admission reason) and want a single factor column instead.

tmp <- data.frame(
  respiratory = sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), 40, replace = TRUE),
  neurologic  = sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), 40, replace = TRUE),
  shock       = sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), 40, replace = TRUE)
)

tmp$reason <- apply(tmp[1:3], 1, function(row) names(tmp)[which(row)])

title: 5  Efficient R Programming
text:
5.1 Timing code
Writing R that runs fast matters as soon as your datasets grow beyond a few thousand rows, or when you run simulations or bootstrap procedures. This chapter covers timing, memory, vectorisation, and parallelism.

title: 5  Efficient R Programming
text:
5.1.1 system.time()
Returns three numbers: user (CPU time for user code), system (CPU time for system calls), and elapsed (wall-clock time). For most purposes, elapsed is what you care about.

colon_fn       <- function(n) 1:n
seq_default    <- function(n) seq(n)
seq_by         <- function(n) seq(1, n, by = 1)

n <- 1e8
system.time(colon_fn(n))
system.time(seq_default(n))
system.time(seq_by(n))

The colon operator is the fastest because it maps directly to a C primitive.


5.1.2 microbenchmark — more precise comparisons

library(microbenchmark)

n <- 1e6
microbenchmark(
  colon    = 1:n,
  seq_def  = seq(n),
  seq_by   = seq(1, n, by = 1),
  times    = 20
)

microbenchmark runs each expression many times and reports summary statistics (min, mean, median, max) in nanoseconds or microseconds.

title: 5  Efficient R Programming
5  Efficient R Programming
text:
5.3 Vectorisation
R’s built-in functions are implemented in C or Fortran and execute on entire vectors at once. Whenever you find yourself writing a loop over a vector, ask whether a vectorised function already exists.

n <- 1e6

# Non-vectorised: one call per element
x <- numeric(n)
for (i in seq_len(n)) x[i] <- rnorm(1)

# Vectorised: one call for all elements
x <- rnorm(n)


microbenchmark(
  loop_version = {
    x <- numeric(n)
    for (i in seq_along(x)) x[i] <- rnorm(1)
  },
  vectorised = rnorm(n),
  times = 3
)

The speedup is typically 100–1000×.

5.3.1 rowSums() and && vs &

# rowSums() is faster than apply(mat, 1, sum)
rowSums(mat)
colSums(mat)
rowMeans(mat)

# && short-circuits (stops evaluating after the first FALSE)
# & always evaluates both sides
if (condition_1 && condition_2) { ... }   # use in if() statements
df |> filter(a & b)                       # use & for vector operations

title: 5  Efficient R Programming
text:
5.4 Matrices vs. data frames
Matrices hold a single data type; data frames can hold multiple. Subsetting a matrix is substantially faster.

n <- 1000
mat <- matrix(rnorm(n * 10), ncol = 10)
df  <- as.data.frame(mat)

microbenchmark(mat[, 1], df[, 1])

When all your data is numeric (e.g. a feature matrix for modelling), convert to a matrix before running computations.

title: 5  Efficient R Programming
text:
5.5 Profiling with profvis
profvis shows a flame graph of where time is spent in a block of code. Wrap any expression in profvis({...}) to visualise it.

library(profvis)
library(ggplot2movies)

profvis({
  comedies <- movies[movies$Comedy == 1, ]
  plot(comedies$year, comedies$rating)
  model <- loess(rating ~ year, data = comedies)
  j <- order(comedies$year)
  lines(comedies$year[j], model$fitted[j], col = "red")
})

Look for wide bars (slow functions) and unexpected calls.

title: 5  Efficient R Programming
text:
5.6 Parallel computing
R is single-threaded by default. The parallel package lets you distribute independent tasks across multiple CPU cores.

5.6.1 When to parallelise
Parallel computing helps when:

Tasks are independent (no iteration \(i\) depends on \(i-1\)) — Monte Carlo simulations, bootstrap resampling, cross-validation folds.
Each task takes at least a few milliseconds (overhead makes it worthless for trivial tasks).



5.6.2 Basic pattern with parApply

library(parallel)

# How many cores are available?
detectCores()

# Create a cluster (leave one core free for the OS)
cl <- makeCluster(detectCores() - 1)

# parApply is a parallel drop-in for apply()
result <- parApply(cl, matrix_data, 2, median)

stopCluster(cl)



5.6.3 parSapply for list/vector inputs

library(parallel)

# A single bootstrap resample
bootstrap <- function(data) {
  idx <- sample(nrow(data), replace = TRUE)
  data[idx, ]
}

cl <- makeCluster(detectCores() - 1)

# Export custom functions and data to each worker
clusterExport(cl, c("bootstrap", "my_data"))

# Run 1000 bootstrap samples in parallel
results <- parSapply(cl, 1:1000, function(i) {
  b <- bootstrap(my_data)
  mean(b$outcome)
})

stopCluster(cl)

text:
5.7 The apply family (single-core)
The apply functions are cleaner alternatives to for loops when working with matrices or lists. They do not automatically speed things up — use them for readability.








Function
Input
Output




apply(X, 1, FUN)
Matrix — apply FUN to each row
Vector or list


apply(X, 2, FUN)
Matrix — apply FUN to each column
Vector or list


sapply(X, FUN)

lapply(X, FUN)
List/vector
Always a list

List/vector
Typed output (safer than sapply)




mat <- matrix(1:12, nrow = 3)
apply(mat, 1, sum)   # row sums
apply(mat, 2, mean)  # column means

sapply(1:5, function(x) x^2)  # c(1, 4, 9, 16, 25)

title: 5  Efficient R Programming
text:
5.8 Error handling and reproducibility

5.8.1 reprex — reproducible examples
When asking for help, always provide a minimal reproducible example. The reprex package formats it for GitHub or Stack Overflow automatically.

y <- 1:4
mean(y)
reprex::reprex()   # copies a formatted snippet to the clipboard



5.8.2 tryCatch — handle errors gracefully

result <- tryCatch(
  expr  = { log(-1) },
  warning = function(w) {
    message("Warning caught: ", conditionMessage(w))
    NA_real_
  },
  error = function(e) {
    message("Error caught: ", conditionMessage(e))
    NA_real_
  }
)

title: 6  Data Visualisation with ggplot2
text:
6.1 The basics
ggplot2 uses a layered grammar of graphics: you build a plot by adding layers (geoms, scales, facets, themes) on top of a base ggplot() call. Extensions for specialised plot types are available at exts.ggplot2.tidyverse.org.

title: 6  Data Visualisation with ggplot2
text:
6.1.1 Anatomy of a ggplot call

ggplot(
  data    = penguins,              # the data frame
  mapping = aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g)  # global aesthetic mapping
) +
  geom_point(aes(color = species, shape = species)) +   # local aesthetic
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  labs(
    title    = "Body mass vs. flipper length",
    subtitle = "Palmer Archipelago penguins",
    x = "Flipper length (mm)",
    y = "Body mass (g)",
    caption  = "Data: palmerpenguins package"
  ) +
  ggthemes::scale_color_colorblind()



6.1.2 Global vs. local aesthetics
Aesthetics specified inside ggplot(aes(...)) apply to all geoms. Aesthetics inside a specific geom_*() apply only to that layer.

# Global: both geom_point and geom_smooth share color = species
penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")

title: 6  Data Visualisation with ggplot2
text:
6.2 Common geoms

6.2.1 Scatter plot — geom_point()

gapminder |>
  filter(year == 2007) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, color = continent, size = pop)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "GDP per capita (log scale)", y = "Life expectancy")










6.2.2 Line plot — geom_line()

gapminder |>
  group_by(year, continent) |>
  summarise(median_gdp = median(gdpPercap), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = median_gdp, color = continent)) +
  geom_line() +
  expand_limits(y = 0)










6.2.3 Histogram — geom_histogram()
Takes a single x aesthetic. Use binwidth to control bin width or bins to set the number of bins.

gapminder |>
  filter(year == 1952) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = pop / 1e6)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "Population (millions, log scale)", y = "Count")










6.2.4 Bar plot — geom_col() vs geom_bar()

geom_bar() counts rows automatically (useful when data has one row per observation).
geom_col() uses a y variable you supply (useful after summarising).


# geom_col() with summarised data
gapminder |>
  filter(year == 1952) |>
  group_by(continent) |>
  summarise(median_gdp = median(gdpPercap)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = continent, y = median_gdp)) +
  geom_col()

# geom_bar() — reorder by frequency
penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_infreq(species))) +
  geom_bar()



6.2.5 Box plot — geom_boxplot()

penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = bill_depth_mm)) +
  geom_boxplot()



6.2.6 Smooth lines — geom_smooth()

ggplot(data, aes(x = dose, y = response)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.05, height = 0.05) +
  geom_smooth(method = "glm", method.args = list(family = "poisson"))

6.7 Overlaying multiple filtered geoms
When you want different subsets of the data on different layers, pass filtered data directly to each geom:

ggplot(data) +
  geom_line(
    data = data |> filter(group == "A"),
    aes(x = time, y = value), color = "steelblue"
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = data |> filter(group == "B"),
    aes(x = time, y = value), color = "tomato"

text:
6.10 Radar / spider charts
The fmsb package draws radar charts from a data frame where the first row is the maximum value per axis and the second row is the minimum.

library(fmsb)

# Build the data frame
scores <- as.data.frame(matrix(
  sample(2:20, 10, replace = TRUE), ncol = 10
))
colnames(scores) <- c("math", "biology", "music", "R", "stats",
                      "french", "physics", "english", "coding", "sport")

# Add max and min rows
scores <- rbind(rep(20, 10), rep(0, 10), scores)

# Default radar chart
radarchart(scores)

# Customised version
radarchart(
  scores,
  axistype  = 1,
  pcol      = rgb(0.2, 0.5, 0.5, 0.9),  # polygon colour
  pfcol     = rgb(0.2, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5),  # fill colour
  plwd      = 3,
  cglcol    = "grey", cglty = 1,
  axislabcol = "grey", caxislabels = seq(0, 20, 5),
  vlcex     = 0.8
)

6.11 Clinical bar plots with custom labels
A pattern that comes up often in clinical papers: side-by-side or stacked bars with percentage labels.

title: 8  Regression & Generalised Linear Models
text:
8.1 Linear models
Generalised linear models (GLMs) extend linear regression to outcomes that are not normally distributed. They share a common framework: a distribution family, a link function, and a linear predictor.
model <- lm(lifeExp ~ gdpPercap + year, data = gapminder)
summary(model)
coef(model)
confint(model)
A linear model is a special case of a GLM with a Gaussian family and identity link.

title: 8  Regression & Generalised Linear Models
text:
8.2 Generalised linear models

# General syntax
glm(formula = y ~ x1 + x2, data = df, family = "binomial")

# Families
glm(y ~ x, data, family = "gaussian")    # same as lm()
glm(y ~ x, data, family = "binomial")    # logistic regression
glm(y ~ x, data, family = "poisson")     # Poisson regression

# Remove the intercept (estimate a coefficient for each group)
glm(y ~ group - 1, data, family = "binomial")

title: 8  Regression & Generalised Linear Models
text:
8.3 Poisson regression
Poisson regression is appropriate for count outcomes, especially when counts are small and contain many zeros.

Coefficients are on the log scale → exponentiate to get the rate ratio.
Poisson coefficients are multiplicative, not additive.


pois_model <- glm(n_events ~ dose + group, data = df, family = "poisson")

# Exponentiate to get rate ratios
exp(coef(pois_model))

# Tidy output with confidence intervals
broom::tidy(pois_model, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)


8.3.1 Plotting a Poisson fit

ggplot(df, aes(x = dose, y = cell_count)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.05, height = 0.05) +
  geom_smooth(method = "glm", method.args = list(family = "poisson"))

title: 8  Regression & Generalised Linear Models
text:
8.4 Logistic regression
Logistic regression models a binary outcome \(Y \in \{0, 1\}\).
Model:
\(\text{logit}(p) = \log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\)
Inverse logit (predicted probability):
\(p = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}}\)

8.4.1 Fitting
Three equivalent data formats:

# 1. Long format (one row per individual, 0/1 outcome)
lr1 <- glm(died ~ age + sofa, data = patients_long, family = "binomial")

# 2. Wide format (successes and failures as separate columns)
lr2 <- glm(cbind(deaths, survivors) ~ age, data = patients_wide, family = "binomial")

# 3. Proportion with weights
lr3 <- glm(mortality_rate ~ age, data = patients_agg, family = "binomial",
           weights = n_total)



8.4.2 Link functions
The default is logit. The probit link is an alternative based on the normal CDF.

glm(y ~ x, family = binomial(link = "logit"))    # default
glm(y ~ x, family = binomial(link = "probit"))

Logit is preferred for outlier-robustness (heavier tails); probit assumes normality.


8.4.3 Interpreting odds ratios

# Extract and exponentiate coefficients
coefs <- coef(model)
exp(coefs)               # odds ratios

# Using broom::tidy — cleaner
broom::tidy(model, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)




OR
Interpretation




> 1
Exposure increases the odds of the outcome


= 1
No effect


< 1
Exposure decreases the odds of the outcome





8.4.4 Visualising logistic regression

ggplot(df, aes(x = age, y = icu_death)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0, height = 0.05) +
  geom_smooth(method = "glm", method.args = list(family = "binomial")) +
  labs(y = "Probability of ICU death")

title: 8  Regression & Generalised Linear Models
text:
8.5 Multiple regression
Rule of thumb: at least 10 events per predictor to avoid overfitting.

model <- glm(
  died ~ age + sofa + mv + vasopressors + creatinine,
  data   = icu_data,
  family = "binomial"
)

summary(model)


8.5.1 Model formula syntax



Formula
Effect




y ~ x
Intercept + slope for x


y ~ x - 1
Slope for x, no intercept


y ~ x1 + x2
Multiple predictors


y ~ x1 * x2
Main effects + interaction


y ~ x1:x2
Interaction only


y ~ .
All columns as predictors





8.5.2 Factor reference levels
The first level of a factor is used as the reference by default (alphabetical order). Change it with relevel():

df$status <- relevel(factor(df$status), ref = "Stable")



8.5.3 Design matrix

model.matrix(~ size)             # reference intercept + contrasts
model.matrix(~ size - 1)         # intercept for each level
model.matrix(~ size + color - 1) # multiple factors, each with own intercept

title: 8  Regression & Generalised Linear Models
text:
8.6 Extracting model results

coef(model)                     # coefficients
confint(model)                  # confidence intervals
predict(model, newdata = df)    # predictions (on link scale)
predict(model, newdata = df, type = "response")  # predictions (probability scale)

# Tidy output (broom package)
broom::tidy(model)
broom::glance(model)            # goodness-of-fit stats
broom::augment(model)           # original data + fitted values + residuals

title: 8  Regression & Generalised Linear Models
text:
8.7 Model assumptions
For logistic regression the key assumptions are:

Linearity in the logit: the log-odds is a linear function of continuous predictors.
Independence of observations: no clustering or repeated measures (without special handling).
No severe multicollinearity: correlated predictors inflate standard errors.
Adequate sample size: ≥ 10 events per predictor.

Watch for overdispersion (more variance than the model expects) and Simpson’s paradox (an important confounding variable missing from the model).

title: 8  Regression & Generalised Linear Models
text:
8.8 Simulating binary data

# Bernoulli: n = number of trials, size = 1 (single coin flip each)
rbinom(n = 100, size = 1, prob = 0.3)

# Binomial: n = 1, size = 100 (one draw of 100 coin flips)
rbinom(n = 1, size = 100, prob = 0.3)

# Convert logit-scale predictions to probability
p <- plogis(0.5)   # = exp(0.5) / (1 + exp(0.5))
rbinom(n = 10, size = 1, prob = p)

title: 9  Survival Analysis
text:
9.1 Core concepts
Survival analysis handles time-to-event outcomes. The key challenge is censoring: some patients have not yet experienced the event at the time of analysis. Standard regression methods cannot handle this correctly — survival methods can.

title: 9  Survival Analysis
text:
Event: the outcome of interest (death, ICU discharge, relapse, etc.)
Censored observation: patient has not experienced the event by the end of follow-up (or was lost to follow-up)
Survival function \(S(t)\): probability of surviving beyond time \(t\)
Hazard function \(h(t)\): instantaneous rate of the event at time \(t\), given survival to \(t\)

title: 9  Survival Analysis
text:
9.2 The Surv object
Every survival analysis starts by creating a Surv object that packages the time and event status together.

# time: follow-up time (numeric)
# event: 1 = event occurred, 0 = censored
sobj <- Surv(time = patients$time, event = patients$status)

# Inspect: + indicates censored observations
sobj[1:10]
summary(sobj)

title: 9  Survival Analysis
text:
9.3 Kaplan–Meier estimator
The Kaplan–Meier estimator is the non-parametric gold standard for estimating the survival function from observed data.

# Overall KM estimate
km <- survfit(Surv(time, event) ~ 1, data = patients)

# By group
km_by_group <- survfit(Surv(time, event) ~ treatment, data = patients)

# Inspect the survfit object
str(km)
km$surv        # estimated survival probabilities
km$time        # times at which the estimate changes
km$n.risk      # number at risk at each time


9.3.1 Plotting with ggsurvplot

ggsurvplot(
  km,
  data             = patients,
  palette          = c("#E41A1C", "#377EB8"),
  surv.median.line = "hv",       # horizontal + vertical lines at median
  conf.int         = TRUE,
  risk.table       = TRUE,       # add risk table below
  cumevents        = TRUE,
  tables.height    = 0.25,
  legend.labs      = c("Control", "Treatment"),
  xlab             = "Time (days)",
  ylab             = "Survival probability"
)



9.3.2 Comparing multiple KM curves

km_a <- survfit(Surv(time, event) ~ 1, data = cohort_a)
km_b <- survfit(Surv(time, event) ~ 1, data = cohort_b)

ggsurvplot_combine(
  list(CohortA = km_a, CohortB = km_b),
  data = patients
)



9.3.3 Log-rank test

# Test whether survival differs between groups
survdiff(Surv(time, event) ~ treatment, data = patients)

title: 9  Survival Analysis
text:
9.4 Cox proportional hazards model
The Cox model estimates how covariates affect the hazard rate, without specifying the baseline hazard function.
\(h(t|X) = h_0(t) \cdot e^{\beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \ldots}\)
Coefficients are log hazard ratios. Exponentiate them to get hazard ratios (HR).

cox <- coxph(Surv(time, event) ~ age + sofa + mv + vasopressors,
             data = icu_data)

summary(cox)

# Extract tidy results
broom::tidy(cox, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)


9.4.1 Interpreting hazard ratios



HR
Interpretation




> 1
Higher hazard (shorter time to event)


= 1
No association


< 1
Lower hazard (longer time to event)





9.4.2 Checking the proportional hazards assumption
The Cox model assumes that the hazard ratio between groups is constant over time.

ph_test <- cox.zph(cox)
print(ph_test)       # p < 0.05 signals a violation
plot(ph_test)        # Schoenfeld residual plots

title: 9  Survival Analysis
text:
9.5 Weibull parametric model
The Weibull model specifies the baseline hazard explicitly, which allows predictions beyond the observed follow-up time.

library(survival)

weibull_model <- survreg(Surv(time, event) ~ age + group,
                         data = patients, dist = "weibull")
summary(weibull_model)

title: 9  Survival Analysis
text:
9.6 Propensity score methods
In observational ICU studies, treatment is rarely randomised. Propensity scores can balance covariates between groups.

library(MatchIt)

# Estimate propensity score and perform 1:1 matching
match_obj <- matchit(
  treatment ~ age + sofa + mv + vasopressors + creatinine,
  data   = icu_data,
  method = "nearest",
  ratio  = 1
)

# Extract matched data
matched_data <- match.data(match_obj)

# Fit Cox model in matched cohort
cox_matched <- coxph(Surv(time, event) ~ treatment,
                     data = matched_data, weights = weights)

10.1 Creating a contingency table
Contingency tables summarise the joint distribution of two or more categorical variables. They are used to test independence and to estimate measures of association.

10.1.1 From individual data

# Direct matrix input
j0 <- c(6, 39)

title: 11  Introduction to Bayesian Data Analysis
text:
11.1 Core vocabulary
Bayesian inference updates a prior distribution (what we believe before seeing data) with observed data to produce a posterior distribution (our updated beliefs).
\[P(\theta | \text{data}) \propto P(\text{data} | \theta) \cdot P(\theta)\]
crumbs: 11  Introduction to Bayesian Data Analysis

title: 11  Introduction to Bayesian Data Analysis
text:
Term
Definition




Prior
\(P(\theta)\) — distribution representing beliefs before data


Likelihood
\(P(\text{data} \| \theta)\) — probability of the data given a parameter value


Posterior
\(P(\theta \| \text{data})\) — updated beliefs after seeing data


Credible interval
Interval that contains the true parameter value with a given probability
crumbs: 11  Introduction to Bayesian Data Analysis

title: 11  Introduction to Bayesian Data Analysis
text:
11.2 Probability distributions in Bayesian analysis

11.2.1 Simulating from a binomial process

# 100 Bernoulli trials with p = 0.42
n_trials    <- 100
prop_success <- 0.42

# Method 1: using runif
data <- as.numeric(runif(n_trials) < prop_success)
sum(data)

# Method 2: using rbinom
rbinom(n = 1,   size = 100, prob = 0.42)   # total successes in 100 trials
rbinom(n = 100, size = 1,   prob = 0.42)   # 100 individual Bernoulli draws



11.2.2 The Beta distribution
The Beta distribution is the natural prior for a probability parameter \(p \in [0, 1]\).

Beta(1, 1) = uniform prior (all values of \(p\) equally likely)
Increasing \(\alpha\) pulls the distribution toward 1; increasing \(\beta\) pulls it toward 0
Larger \(\alpha + \beta\) → narrower distribution (more prior certainty)


# Uninformative prior
beta_uniform <- rbeta(1000, shape1 = 1, shape2 = 1)
hist(beta_uniform, main = "Beta(1,1) - Uniform prior", xlab = "p")

# Informative prior: believe click-through rate ~5%
beta_informative <- rbeta(1000, shape1 = 5, shape2 = 95)
hist(beta_informative, main = "Beta(5, 95) - Informative prior", xlab = "p")
crumbs: 11  Introduction to Bayesian Data Analysis

title: 11  Introduction to Bayesian Data Analysis
text:
11.3 A complete Bayesian workflow
This example models the click-through rate of an advertisement.

set.seed(42)
n_draws       <- 100000
n_ads_shown   <- 100
observed_clicks <- 13

# Step 1: Sample from the prior
proportion_clicks <- rbeta(n_draws, shape1 = 5, shape2 = 95)

# Step 2: Simulate outcomes under the prior
n_visitors <- rbinom(n_draws, size = n_ads_shown, prob = proportion_clicks)

prior <- data.frame(proportion_clicks, n_visitors)

# Step 3: Condition on observed data (posterior ≈ those simulations matching observation)
posterior <- prior[prior$n_visitors == observed_clicks, ]

# Step 4: Summarise the posterior
cat("Posterior median:", median(posterior$proportion_clicks), "\n")
cat("95% credible interval:", quantile(posterior$proportion_clicks, c(0.025, 0.975)), "\n")
cat("P(rate > 0.10):", mean(posterior$proportion_clicks > 0.10), "\n")


# Visualise prior vs posterior
par(mfrow = c(2, 1))
hist(prior$proportion_clicks,     xlim = c(0, 0.25), main = "Prior", xlab = "p")
hist(posterior$proportion_clicks, xlim = c(0, 0.25), main = "Posterior", xlab = "p")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
crumbs: 11  Introduction to Bayesian Data Analysis

title: 11  Introduction to Bayesian Data Analysis
text:
11.4 Interpreting the posterior

median(posterior)               # point estimate
quantile(posterior, c(0.05, 0.95))   # 90% credible interval
sum(posterior > 0.07) / length(posterior)  # P(p > 0.07)


11.4.1 Credible interval vs. confidence interval

A 95% credible interval says: “There is a 95% probability that the true parameter lies in this interval.” This is the intuitive frequentist interpretation that people mistakenly apply to confidence intervals.
A 95% confidence interval says: “If we repeated this experiment many times, 95% of the intervals constructed this way would contain the true value.”

title: 12  Factor Analysis & Structural Equation Modelling
text:
12.1 Key concepts
Factor analysis is a set of techniques for discovering latent constructs (factors) that explain correlations among observed variables (items). It underpins the validation and scoring of psychometric scales, including instruments commonly used in clinical research such as the HADS.
crumbs: 12  Factor Analysis & Structural Equation Modelling

title: 12  Factor Analysis & Structural Equation Modelling
text:
Concept
Definition




Latent variable
An unobserved construct inferred from observed items (e.g. “Anxiety”)


Factor loading
Correlation between an item and a factor


Communality
Proportion of an item’s variance explained by the factors


EFA
Exploratory FA — no prior theory about which items load on which factors


CFA
Confirmatory FA — tests a specific hypothesised factor structure
crumbs: 12  Factor Analysis & Structural Equation Modelling

title: 12  Factor Analysis & Structural Equation Modelling
text:
12.2 Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA)

12.2.1 When to use EFA
Use EFA when you do not have a strong prior theory about the factor structure, or when you are developing a new scale.


12.2.2 Running an EFA

library(psych)

# Single-factor EFA
efa_1 <- fa(hads_data)
efa_1
efa_1$loadings

# Multi-factor EFA
efa_3 <- fa(hads_data, nfactors = 3)
efa_3$loadings
head(efa_3$scores)

# Path diagram
fa.diagram(efa_3, labels = colnames(hads_data))



12.2.3 Descriptive statistics for items

describe(hads_data)      # mean, SD, skew, kurtosis for each item
error.bars(hads_data)    # error bar plot
error.dots(hads_data)    # dot plot with error bars



12.2.4 Determining the number of factors
Eigenvalue criterion (Kaiser rule): retain factors with eigenvalue > 1.

# Scree plot
item_cor   <- cor(hads_data, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
eigen_vals <- eigen(item_cor)
eigen_vals$values

psych::scree(item_cor, factors = FALSE)
crumbs: 12  Factor Analysis & Structural Equation Modelling

title: 12  Factor Analysis & Structural Equation Modelling
text:
12.3 Reliability

12.3.1 Cronbach’s alpha
Measures internal consistency — the extent to which items in a scale measure the same construct. A commonly cited threshold is α > 0.80 for good reliability.

alpha_result <- psych::alpha(hads_data)
alpha_result$total$raw_alpha

# Split-half reliability
psych::splitHalf(hads_data)



12.3.2 Correlation matrix

# Base R
lowerCor(hads_data)
corr.test(hads_data, use = "pairwise.complete.obs", method = "pearson", adjust = "none")

# Correlogram with ggcorrplot
library(ggcorrplot)
p_mat <- cor_pmat(hads_data, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")

hads_data |>
  cor(use = "pairwise.complete.obs") |>
  ggcorrplot(
    hc.order    = TRUE,
    type        = "upper",
    lab         = TRUE,
    p.mat       = p_mat,
    sig.level   = 0.01,
    insig       = "blank",
    colors      = c("tomato2", "white", "springgreen3")
  )
crumbs: 12  Factor Analysis & Structural Equation Modelling

title: 12  Factor Analysis & Structural Equation Modelling
text:
12.4 Splitting data for EFA/CFA
Best practice: run EFA on half the data, CFA on the other half.

set.seed(42)
N       <- nrow(scale_data)
idx_efa <- sample(seq_len(N), floor(0.5 * N))
idx_cfa <- setdiff(seq_len(N), idx_efa)

data_efa <- scale_data[idx_efa, ]
data_cfa <- scale_data[idx_cfa, ]
crumbs: 12  Factor Analysis & Structural Equation Modelling

title: 12  Factor Analysis & Structural Equation Modelling
text:
12.5 Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA)
CFA tests a theoretically specified factor structure using the lavaan package.

12.5.1 Model specification

library(lavaan)

# Two-factor model (lavaan syntax)
model_hads <- "
  Depression =~ HADS_DEP_Q8 + HADS_DEP_Q9 + HADS_DEP_Q10 +
                HADS_DEP_Q11 + HADS_DEP_Q12 + HADS_DEP_Q13 + HADS_DEP_Q14
  Anxiety    =~ HADS_ANX_Q1 + HADS_ANX_Q2 + HADS_ANX_Q3 +
                HADS_ANX_Q4 + HADS_ANX_Q5 + HADS_ANX_Q6 + HADS_ANX_Q7
"

fit <- cfa(model_hads, data = hads_data, std.lv = TRUE)
summary(fit, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)



12.5.2 Model fit indices



Index
Good fit




CFI (Comparative Fit Index)
> 0.90


TLI (Tucker–Lewis Index)
> 0.90


RMSEA
< 0.05


SRMR
< 0.08




fitMeasures(fit, c("cfi", "tli", "rmsea", "srmr", "aic", "bic"))



12.5.3 Comparing two models

# Likelihood-ratio test (only valid for nested models on the same data)
anova(fit_short, fit_full)

# BIC comparison (lower = better)
fitMeasures(fit_short, "bic")
fitMeasures(fit_full, "bic")



12.5.4 McDonald’s omega
Omega is a more accurate reliability estimate than Cronbach’s alpha when factor loadings are unequal.

omega_result <- psych::omega(hads_data, nfactors = 2)
omega_result$omega.tot

title: 12  Factor Analysis & Structural Equation Modelling
text:
12.6 Cross-validation of a CFA model

library(cvTools)

k    <- 5
set.seed(123)
folds <- cvFolds(nrow(data_cfa), K = k)

cv_results <- data.frame(Fold = 1:k, CFI = NA, RMSEA = NA, SRMR = NA)

for (i in seq_len(k)) {
  test_idx  <- which(folds$which == i)
  train_dat <- data_cfa[-test_idx, ]
  fit_cv    <- cfa(model_hads, data = train_dat, std.lv = TRUE)
  fm        <- fitMeasures(fit_cv, c("cfi", "rmsea", "srmr"))
  cv_results[i, c("CFI", "RMSEA", "SRMR")] <- fm
}

colMeans(cv_results[, -1], na.rm = TRUE)

title: 12  Factor Analysis & Structural Equation Modelling
text:
12.7 Finding optimal scale cutoffs
When shortening a scale, you need to derive new cutoffs for the reduced score. The approach below finds the cutoff on the short scale that maximises Cohen’s kappa agreement with the full-scale categories.

library(irr)

# Assume full-scale scores and categories are already computed
# Find optimal binary cutoff for the shortened scale
kappa_vals <- sapply(0:12, function(thresh) {
  short_case <- short_scores >= thresh
  if (length(unique(short_case)) == 2) {
    kappa2(data.frame(full_case, short_case))$value
  } else NA
})

best_cutoff <- which.max(kappa_vals) - 1   # adjust for 0-indexing
cat("Best cutoff:", best_cutoff, "| Kappa:", max(kappa_vals, na.rm = TRUE))


12.7.1 ROC-based cutoff selection

library(pROC)

roc_obj   <- roc(full_case, short_scores, direction = "<")
auc(roc_obj)

best_coords <- coords(roc_obj, x = "best", best.method = "youden",
                      ret = c("threshold", "sensitivity", "specificity"))
print(best_coords)

title: 13  Machine Learning in R
text:
13.1 The caret package
This chapter covers practical machine learning workflows in R, focusing on the tools most relevant for clinical and research applications.
caret (Classification And REgression Training) provides a unified interface for training and evaluating hundreds of models. It handles cross-validation, hyperparameter tuning, and pre-processing consistently across methods.
library(caret)

# Split into training and test sets
set.seed(42)
train_idx <- createDataPartition(df$outcome, p = 0.8, list = FALSE)
train_dat <- df[ train_idx, ]
test_dat  <- df[-train_idx, ]

# Define cross-validation scheme
ctrl <- trainControl(
  method    = "cv",
  number    = 10,
  classProbs = TRUE,
  summaryFunction = twoClassSummary
)

# Train a model (e.g. random forest)
model <- train(
  outcome ~ .,
  data      = train_dat,
  method    = "rf",
  trControl = ctrl,
  metric    = "ROC"
)

print(model)
varImp(model)   # variable importance

# Predict on test set
preds <- predict(model, newdata = test_dat)
confusionMatrix(preds, test_dat$outcome)

title: 13  Machine Learning in R
text:
13.2 Gradient boosting with XGBoost
XGBoost is the go-to algorithm for structured tabular data. It builds an ensemble of decision trees sequentially, each correcting the errors of the previous one.

13.2.1 Cross-validation to find the optimal number of trees

library(xgboost)

cv <- xgb.cv(
  data              = as.matrix(train_features),
  label             = train_labels,
  nrounds           = 200,
  nfold             = 5,
  objective         = "reg:squarederror",  # or "binary:logistic"
  eta               = 0.1,     # learning rate
  max_depth         = 6,
  early_stopping_rounds = 10,
  verbose           = 0
)

# Find optimal number of trees
elog     <- cv$evaluation_log
ntrees   <- elog$iter[which.min(elog$test_rmse_mean)]
cat("Optimal trees:", ntrees)



13.2.2 Training and prediction

model_xgb <- xgboost(
  data      = as.matrix(train_features),
  label     = train_labels,
  nrounds   = ntrees,
  objective = "reg:squarederror",
  eta       = 0.1,
  max_depth = 6,
  verbose   = 0
)

# Predict
test_data$pred <- predict(model_xgb, as.matrix(test_features))

# Evaluate (regression: RMSE)
test_data |>
  mutate(residuals = outcome - pred) |>
  summarise(rmse = sqrt(mean(residuals^2)))



13.2.3 Visualise predictions vs. actuals

ggplot(test_data, aes(x = pred, y = outcome)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "tomato") +
  labs(x = "Predicted", y = "Observed")

13.3.1 Classification metrics

14.2 The workflow: input → server → output
User interacts with input widget
    ↓
input$id changes value
    ↓
server recomputes output$id
    ↓
Output renders in the UI

Inputs are always defined in the UI and accessed in the server as input$inputId.
Outputs are rendered in the server and displayed in the UI via *Output() functions.

14.3 UI elements

14.3.1 Layout functions



Function
Purpose




fluidPage()
Fluid layout (adjusts to browser width)


fixedPage()
Fixed-width layout


navbarPage()
Page with navigation tabs


sidebarLayout()
Two-column layout with sidebar + main area


sidebarPanel()
Sidebar column


mainPanel()
Main column


tabsetPanel() + tabPanel()
Tabbed panels within a page





14.3.2 Standard layout with sidebar

ui <- fluidPage(
  titlePanel("My Clinical Dashboard"),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      textInput("name", "Patient name:"),
      sliderInput("age", "Age:", min = 0, max = 120, value = 50),
      selectInput("group", "Group:", choices = c("Control", "Treated"))
    ),
    mainPanel(
      plotOutput("survival_plot"),
      tableOutput("summary_table")
    )
  )
)

# Slider with animation button
sliderInput("year", "Year:", min = 2000, max = 2024, value = 2010, animate = TRUE)

# Dropdown with grouped choices
selectInput(
  "species",
  "Select species:",
  choices = list(
    Penguins = list("Adelie", "Chinstrap", "Gentoo"),
    Others   = list("Emperor", "King")
  )
)

# Text input with placeholder
textInput("query", label = "", placeholder = "Search patient ID...")
